en: Continuation of the *Fuzongji* (Collection on Returning to the Source), Lower Volume: White Lotus of the Eastern Aile;
in response to Xian, describing the sands of *upāya* for teaching and realization.

Regarding the distinction between the cultivation and realization, as well as the teaching and the evidence, of the Pure Land, Jingxi stated: "In the former two teachings, both the teaching and the evidence are provisional; in the Perfect Teaching, both the teaching and the evidence are entirely real."
The provisional teaching of the Separate Vehicle (*biejiao*) regarding the realization of truth is somewhat difficult to understand, and many people are confused by it.

For this reason, our school borrows the meaning of "teaching" and "realization" from the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Ten Stages) to clarify the Separate Gate; thus, there arise four aspects categorized according to practice and according to teaching.

Tracing back the origin of the Tiantai school’s borrowing [of these concepts], it was solely for the purpose that the provisional teaching and realization of the Separate Vehicle—rather than its stages—are difficult to elucidate.

In the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), the teaching path (*jiaodao*) is provisional while the realization path (*zhengdao*) is real; this meaning is quite consistent and can be borrowed for the purpose of analytical interpretation.
When taking various teachings as examples, the stages and positions of each respective practice also possess both provisional and real meanings, as they can all be universally applied.

Thus, the *Yili* (Principles of Meaning) states: "The two paths of teaching and realization originally belong to the Separate Teaching, yet they may also be used universally; therefore, they are distinguished according to two senses."
Regarding the reason why the explanation based on realization is universally applicable, it concerns both the path of teaching and the path of realization.

As for the division into two meanings, these four types must be clarified within the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*). Although many predecessors of old have spoken of this, those who have clearly elucidated it are few.
I have long harbored doubts regarding this principle; however, through reflection, I have finally attained understanding and realized that all the various arguments of the past...

Regarding what has not yet been established: traditionally, when distinguishing between the path of practice (*caryā-mārga*) and the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*) based on teaching and realization, the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) is taken as the teaching and the attainment of the grounds (*bhūmi-praviṣṭa*) as the realization.
When discussing the teaching and realization in terms of exposition, it is invariably stated that these are taught for those prior to the grounds.

The entirety of the beginning and end of a single teaching is termed the "path of teaching" (*deśanā-mārga*), while the exposition of the dharmas of the ten grounds is termed the "path of realization" (*adhigama-mārga*). Although each employs its own literary style, they are all categorized according to the path of practice and teaching.

The realization and the summary exposition of the path of teaching are identical for all; it is only in the summary exposition of the path of realization that there are differences—some say it expounds the ten stages as perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), while others say it expounds them as sequentially distinct (*gelie*). What is discussed here now differs fundamentally from what was previously held.
Only by clarifying this through the sūtras and śāstras and examining it against the patriarchal texts can one see that the present exposition accords with what is correct and appropriate.
First, let us examine the ancient expositions to clearly see where they fall short, so that we may then reveal the present meaning as being in accord with the Patriarch’s own text.
For instance, regarding the fourfold [teachings] within the fifty-two stages from beginning to end in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*):

the stage prior to the grounds (*diqian*) is discussed in terms of the path of practice and teaching (*xingjiaodao*), while the attainment of the grounds (*dengdi*) is discussed in terms of the path of realization and proof (*zhengdaodao*). Furthermore, when discussing the paths of teaching and proof (*shuojiaodao* and *shuzhengdao*), it is again by way of explanation...

The beginning and end of the One Teaching are explained in terms of the Path of Teaching (*śāsanamārga*), while the exposition of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) is explained in terms of the Path of Realization (*adhigamamārga*).

In this way, there are only three types [of stages] that can be subsumed under the categories of practice and position (*pratipattisthāna*), because there are three kinds: those prior to the stages (*bhūmipūrva*), those within the stages (*bhūmistha*), and those beyond the stages (*bhūmyuttara*).

One type is the general exposition of the Dharma (which explains the One Teaching in terms of the Path of Teaching). Thus, it is sufficient to borrow these three types to distinguish the gates, practices, and positions. Why?
If one speaks of the path of teaching in brief, it is seen that this single method is used to determine which stage possesses what function.
For instance, when the Buddhas of the various teachings expound the Dharma, they do so entirely for the sake of beginners;

thus, the beginning and end of their fundamental teachings, as well as their stages and positions of practice, must all be explained in terms of the path of teaching. How much more so is this true for the stages and positions of practice within the four teachings?
This is simply because, within the Great Canon of the Tathāgata’s lifetime of teaching— comprising the sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras— all are proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata himself,
or expounded by bodhisattvas and sages on his behalf. Regarding the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and abandonment (*prahāṇa*),

they must all be understood as explanations concerning the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), for there is nothing therein that does not exhaustively explain the stages of practice for those of initial resolve.
Since these are equal dharmas, how is it that you are so utterly ignorant as to never even slightly contemplate and investigate them in this way?
Not only is the borrowing by our own school useless, but one also sees that the explanations in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* are superficial and lack essential brevity;

what is the use of borrowing from them? Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the realization of the Way (*bodhi-mārga*), since both the beginning and end of a single teaching [are covered], [the borrowing is redundant].
If this is explained in terms of the path of teaching (*deśanāmārga*), then the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are already included therein;

furthermore, if it is explained in terms of the path of realization (*adhigamamārga*) by way of the ten stages, then it refers to the two successive turnings of the Dharma wheel by the Tathāgata. Thus, the meanings of all the various positions are each twofold.

This is why some masters treat the ten stages as being perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), while others treat them as being sequential and distinct (*gelil*), based on the intent of these two successive teachings.

The Dharma is divided into two meanings: first, regarding the path of teaching (*deśanā-mārga*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are explained as sequential and distinct; second, regarding the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*), the ten stages are explained as perfectly interfused.
Because one wishes to distinguish these two meanings within a single stage of practice, it is unavoidable that such an explanation must be made.
Tracing the source of this error, it lies in not understanding the two types of nomenclature and instead asserting that the explanation regarding the practitioner follows from their actual conduct.
Regarding the term "approximate explanation" (*yōsetsu*) derived from the context of human biographies: it is named based on the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.

Because of this, erroneous interpretations have arisen, leading to distortions in the classification and subsumption of the stages and practices (*gyōi*) taught therein. This malady has persisted for a long time;

later generations have followed this habit, mistaking error for truth without ever realizing it. Within the Four Teachings (*shikyō*), everything is nothing other than the preaching of the Dharma and nothing other than the practice of the Way.

Regarding the practice (*caryā*), why is this meaning treated as distinct? Although all [categories] generally apply to both the specific and the general, the primary application here concerns the ordinary discourse on doctrinal principles (*śāsana-artha*).
First, one must correctly establish the terminology; if the terminology is incorrect, the meaning will become obstructed. As the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states:

"The preceding passage refers to practice (*caryā*), while the subsequent passage refers to teaching (*śāsana*). The *Fuxingji* (Supplementary Commentary) states: "First, it refers to practice; second, it refers to the exposition of meaning. The *Yili* (Exemplification of Principles) states: "It refers to..."
These explanations are made in terms of realization (*pratyātmavedana*). Thus, one knows that various passages refer to either practice (*caryā*), teaching (*śāsana*), or realization.
Some say "in terms of practice" and some say "in terms of realization"; this is because there are those who progress through the stages of cultivation and those who have already attained realization.

Regarding the explanations in terms of teaching and realization, some say "in terms of teaching" and some say "in terms of exposition"; this is because there are cases where only the teaching exists and no one has yet progressed through the stages.
The claim that people realize the fruits of the path is empty talk intended only to entice the capacities of sentient beings;

therefore, it is called "provisional according to discourse" (*yue-shuo*). This does not mean taking the Tathāgata’s actual preaching as provisional discourse. Rather, these discourses are merely skillful means (*upāya*) established within the gates of the teaching; such discourses are termed "provisional according to discourse.
If one does not correctly attach the names to the two types of categories and explains the meanings accordingly, all will be erroneous. If one relies on the explanations...
To say that there is only the teaching (*śāsana*) and no person (*pudgala*) means that the path of both teaching and realization (*śikṣā-adhigama-mārga*) has already been traversed by half.

Once this is understood, one may then discuss the correlation between the four stages of practice (*caturvidha-pratipatti-sthāna*) and the fifty-two positions of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), thereby clarifying the distinct gate.

Regarding the correlation of practice, teaching, and realization: the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) belong to the teaching, while ascending the grounds belongs to realization; this is as explained in the *Xuán*.

The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) clearly states that the divisions of the text are evident and universally accepted by all, with little cause for confusion. However, regarding the classification based on the "Teaching" (*jiao*) and "Realization" (*zheng*), many people are deluded;

therefore, it is now necessary to establish the distinctions according to the stages of practice (*xing*) and positions (*wei*). Only then will one realize that previous explanations were entirely uncomprehending.

One must know that the entirety of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) from beginning to end constitutes the "Teaching" (*jiao*) path, while the Single [Stage] of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) constitutes the "Realization" (*zheng*) path.

The stages (*bhūmi*) are explained in brief as being realized only upon the Path of Realization (*darśana-mārga*). By means of these four types of teaching and realization, the distinct teachings (*pratyeka-śāsana*) and their respective stages of practice and realization are distinguished so that they do not become confused.

Thus, within the Distinct Teaching (*bhedaka-śāsana*), if one speaks in terms of practice, teaching, and realization regarding the "true" versus the "semblance," this refers to the contrast between the stages prior to the *bhūmis* (*pṛthak-bhūmi*) and those who have entered the *bhūmis*.
If one speaks in terms of the division of teaching and realization regarding the "extreme" (*koṭi*) versus the "limited" (*anta*), this refers to the ten [stages].
When the stages (*bhūmi*) and wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) are discussed in relation to practice and teaching, each has its own distinct rank and boundaries;

thus, one avoids the fallacy of a single position belonging to two categories. Furthermore, how can one see that when discussing the teachings and proofs, [the path] proceeds from the stages upward without involving the pre-stage levels?
The clear texts of the Patriarchs are not obscure; yet those with eyes clearly remain deluded. Now, for their sake...

It points out that the current meaning has a specific destination; the *Shiqian* (Signpost) states: "Relying on the meaning of the path of teaching (*jiaodao*), the Dharma for those who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) is explained by means of the four *siddhāntas*;
therefore, it is known that from the first stage upward, the path of teaching still persists. The *Fuxing* (Aids to Practice) explains:

"Second, regarding the explanation [of the stages], they are spoken of as being prior to the stages; from beginning to end, they belong to the teaching. This clarifies that the dharmas of the stages themselves constitute the teaching."

The Way does not involve the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*); former scholars all erroneously misinterpreted the beginning and end of the *Fuxing wen* as referring to the beginning and end of a single teaching, thereby falling into fallacy.
They failed to realize that what is called "beginning and end" refers to the beginning and end of the ten grounds, not the beginning and end of a single teaching.
How is this known? By citing the original text of the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* to illuminate it, one will finally see it now.

It is said that this truly captures the essential meaning of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*. Within the *Śāstra*, when Vajragarbha Bodhisattva arose from samādhi and expounded the Dharma of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), there were twenty phrases.
The eleventh phrase states: "Furthermore, because there is a beginning and end to the ten grounds of the bodhisattvas. The *Śāstra* then says:
"That which is called 'attaining the beginning and end of the bodhisattva's ten grounds' refers to this fundamental beginning and end (and so forth, up to) the beginning of the ten meanings."
The *Zhonglun Mingwen* (Explanatory Text on the Final Treatise) states that the beginning and end of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) do not constitute a single teaching;

how could this clear text not take the ten stages as its scope for explaining the path of teaching? The *Jiaodian* (Signpost of the Teaching Path) says: "Thus we know that from the first stage upward, the path of teaching still persists"—this is precisely what is meant here.
How could it ever have been intended that the path of teaching explained by way of summary applies to those prior to the stages? Failing to see this, [some] immediately...
To interpret the beginning and end of a single teaching by attempting to reconcile its textual expressions—how much error lies therein!

Often, when people encounter passages stating that [certain practices] "still exist," they conclude that what exists prior to the Grounds (*bhūmi*) is already the Path of Teaching (*jiaodao*), and that what remains on the Grounds is likewise so. Is this not to claim that the beginning and end of a single teaching are both merely provisional explanations?

They fail to understand that Jingxi’s intention was to mean that what exists prior to the Grounds is a provisional explanation regarding the practice of the Path of Teaching, while what exists on the Grounds is the actual Path of Teaching itself.

From the above, it is clear that while the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*) has been established, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) still pertain to the provisional teaching of the path of doctrine (*deśanā-mārga*).

Is this not to say that even upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*), the path of doctrine still persists? Thus, it becomes even more evident that the stage prior to the grounds refers to the provisional teaching of the path of practice (*pratipatti-mārga*), while the stages themselves refer to the provisional teaching of the path of doctrine.

Furthermore, the reference to the "provisional teaching of the path of realization" pointing toward the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue-wei*) is as stated in the *Shu*: "If one speaks of the ten..."

The dharmas already realized on the stages (*bhūmi*) are precisely the Path of Realization (*bodhimārga*). Since it is said they are "already realized," one must ask: who is this person who has already realized them?
Regarding the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), there are various texts that either affirm or deny its existence; for now, we shall set aside such debates.

What is intended here is the person of the fruit of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) as the one who has already realized the ten stages. However, I urge you to carefully examine the single character "already" (*yi*).
Now, seeing that the established symbols and their meanings coincide, how can this be known? Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* states:
"The Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment (doctrang) is precisely the meaning of realizing the Way; what is attained at the site of enlightenment is it not wondrous awakening (miaojue)?

In the *Fuxing*, it is said that severing the twelve grades of ignorance is termed wondrous awakening. These are precisely explanations concerning the realization of the Way; how could there be any [severance] apart from this?
Regarding the Buddha who has severed twelve grades of ignorance: according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the Buddha merely severs these twelve grades.
From the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) and its realization of reality, the first ground (prathamā bhūmi) is identical to the first dwelling (prathama-vihāra).

Thus, one knows that from the grounds upward, there exists only the path of teaching (jiaodao), while the person of realization (xingzhengzhe) is found only at the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (myōgaku). Therefore, the ten grounds constitute the path of teaching.
If the realization of the Way is truly devoid of persons and consists only of its teachings, then these stages of practice and positions would all become mere empty constructs.

Whether regarding the teaching or the realization, they are all termed "provisional explanations" (*yueshuo*). It is precisely because the provisional and the real within the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) are difficult to clarify that one borrows those meanings to dissolve the Separate Gate;
only then does one see the efficacy of the four kinds of borrowed meanings, which have long been misunderstood by previous masters.
One who understands this meaning realizes it emerges from the present; it is not an act of self-conceit, but rather accords with the intent of the Patriarchs.
Alas! This principle was made exceedingly clear by the Patriarchal Masters; why do people remain so ignorant? Now that we have finally attained this vision, how could we not rejoice?

Thus, we know that within our own school, those four types [of teachings] are borrowed merely to distinguish one teaching; furthermore, there is neither the fault of overlapping stages nor any need for further borrowing.

There is no fault of meritlessness, nor is there the error of the various teachings being promiscuously conflated; I ask those who study the teachings to examine this in detail with an impartial mind.
Question: Since the "abbreviated teaching path" (yōsetsu kyōdō) begins with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) must be the beginning of the abbreviated teaching path;
furthermore, since it is also the beginning of the "abbreviated path of practice and realization" (yōgyū shōdō), is it not simply one and the same stage?

There are still two categories; if one were to say otherwise, it should be explained that the path of teaching and practice can only discuss the beginning and end of nine stages (*navabhūmi*), and one should not speak of ten.

The answer to this is that this single stage represents the divergence between the progressive approach of the *Ekayāna* (One Vehicle) and the distinction between the *Vaipulya* (Perfect) and *Vibhajya* (Separate) teachings;

it is truly not easy to understand, and many people are confused by it. There is a profound reason for using that [concept] as a criterion for interpretation, for it concerns the initial mind (*ādikarmika-citta*).

According to the teachings, the exhaustion of the twelve grades of ignorance is taken as the stage of the ultimate fruit (*phala*), while the first grade of the first stage (*bhūmi*) is taken as the realization of the partial fruit.
Upon entering the first grade of the stages, the [delusory] obstructions are just extinguished and one clearly perceives the perfect principle;

thus, the first stage is identical to the first dwelling (*vihāra*). Nevertheless, because this has come from the prior stages through sequential cultivation and realization, it is still categorized according to the original aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

To speak in terms of actual realization refers to the stage of the path of realization in the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*). If one proceeds from entering the stages (*bhūmi*) to dwell in common with others, one belongs to those at the first *abhisamaya* of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*);

one no longer holds the office of the first stage of the Separate Teaching. Consequently, the single stage of the first ground would likewise be devoid of practitioners and thus rendered a hollow fiction.
For this reason, this stage still belongs to the path of teaching (*jiaodao*). Therefore, the *Zhi guan* states: "Within the cause..."
Regarding the teaching, practice, realization, and the person who attains the fruit: in this [teaching], there is only the teaching, but no practice, realization, or person who attains the fruit.

When one breaks through ignorance and ascends to the first stage (*bhūmi*), this is precisely the position of the first dwelling (*vihāra*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), and not the first stage of the Separate Teaching (*biejia*).

If this is so even for the first stage, how much more so for the subsequent fruits? The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "If even the first stage is non-existent [in that sense], how much more so the subsequent fruits? Regarding the first stage, one enters and dwells therein.
This is the main text; one need not doubt its status as a teaching-path (śāsana-mārga) discourse.

Therefore, although from the perspective of the teaching path the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) appears to have no actual person who attains it, it is said that from the beginning to the end of the ten stages, it is attained from the perspective of the realization path (*adhigama-mārga*).

That this is a distinct individual who enters this station is the meaning of the term "realization path"; in fact, it is identical to the title received at the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*). One should reflect upon this in order to understand it.

Question: If one speaks of the Path of Teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) and the Path of Realization (*adhigama-mārga*) by way of "having the teaching but no person," then since the Buddhas who are the fruits of the first two teachings also possess the teaching but lack a person, should they also be considered as speaking of the Path of Realization by way of this same principle? Answer: The two paths of Teaching and Realization are fundamentally distinct;

the former is the provisional teaching (*upāya-śāsana*), while the latter is the realization of truth (*tattva-adhigama*). Therefore, they are employed [differently]. If one were to apply this analogy to all teachings, they could indeed be used interchangeably.

There is also an interpretation based on practice, teaching, and realization; furthermore, when seeking the fruit through its meaning, the Buddha may also be understood as such through this conventional explanation of the path of realization.

This is because there is no person who realizes it by practicing from a cause; however, what is presented here is not that case, as it is not the primary intent of borrowing the terms "teaching" and "realization.
Since the fruit of the former teaching was originally one, yet the Buddha manifested it as three traces, we now temporarily borrow these terms for the sake of explanation.

In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the provisional and real aspects of the teachings, the realization, the practice, and the stages are distinguished according to their provisional and real natures; other matters are not essential here, so why borrow them?

It is because people have not seen this point that they take the four types of teaching-realization as a model to apply them universally across the Four Teachings—this is a failure to grasp the underlying principle.
Furthermore, seeing that the text of the *Yili* (Exemplification of Meanings) states they may be applied universally, they then divide it into two meanings and apply the Four Teachings accordingly.
The statement that "all four types are universally applicable" refers to the passage concerning delusion, as has already been explained previously.

That they are now also said to be "universally applicable" means that the two paths—teaching and realization—are used to distinguish between the provisional and the real. Regarding the division into two meanings:

within the "Correct Teaching" (*biete jiao*), this concerns both the exposition and the practice. This can be understood through reflection. Question: Regarding the path of realization, is it provisional or real? If one says it is...

Quan Xuanwen borrows those two types [of teachings] to establish the reality of the *zhengbu* (the section on realization). If it is said that this is "real," yet there is only teaching and no practice or person who realizes it, how can it be real?
The traditional explanation says: regarding the teaching of the path of realization, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are explained as being perfectly interfused, like the divine wisdom.
Xuan says: regarding the teaching of the path of realization, the person who is able to teach it is a Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

The Dharma taught is the perfectly integrated (yuanrong) Dharma; the persons for whom it is intended are those who are directed toward the perfect (yuan) while practicing the distinct (bie). Master Yuan’s commentary explains: "In terms of the teaching and realization paths, it is for the sake of those with the capacity for the perfect and real (yuan-shi) at the stages of abiding, practice, and advancement prior to the distinct grounds (*bhūmi*). Because the Tathāgata responds to them, he teaches the perfectly integrated Dharma of the ten grounds to receive and guide them. Master Lun’s *Jingwei* further states: ... [text continues] ... ... There is a class of people who claim that those before the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*) should hear of the "perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*) of the realization of the Way (*zhengdao*), which is attached to what they previously received regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as being sequential;

they point out this perfect fusion and call it an "explanation according to [the provisional] teaching. All such assertions claim that these are teachings on the perfect fusion of the ten stages as a reality.
If we examine this with our current judgment, can such a thing be possible? It is clear that they have not understood the meaning of "an explanation according to [the provisional] teaching" at all.
The purport of this is that it is merely a provisional designation. Master Zhan said: "Of the four kinds of teaching and realization, three are provisional and one is real;
this is based solely on the path of realization through practice being real. If so, then regarding the path of realization through verbal explanation, it should also be provisional.

If that is the case, why is it said to realize the truth? There are two meanings: first, because the provisional is used to realize the real, it is specifically called 'borrowed'; if it were exclusively [provisional],..."
In truth, why is it necessary to say "borrowed"? Because the two aspects are mutually interdependent, they serve as evidence; thus it is said, "and by means of the path of realization.

However, while this interpretation—that one can know the three provisional [teachings] and the one reality—is superior to those of other masters, it still fails to recognize that the "path of realization" spoken of here refers to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It is a case of mistaking the near for the far; therefore, it is not accepted here. As for the arguments of the various masters, they are entirely devoid of insight. If...

This means: for one who practices the perfect [teaching], why is it said that they preach the perfectly interfused Dharma? Why is it called "entering the stages" (*bhūmi*) when the gate of self-realization opens of its own accord?

If you say this refers to those who are "received" [into the path], what kind of reception is it? If it were a perfect reception of the distinct [teaching], one should speak of the perfectly interfused Dharma of the fifty-two stages of the Perfect Teaching;
what need would there be for the perfectly interfused ten stages? If it were a distinct reception, it would be exactly as [stated by] Jingxi [Zhanran].
The stream is broken by clouds, forming separate connections; being thus connected three times, it cannot be gathered back. Therefore, one knows how utterly inverted was the ancient claim of "one.

One must understand that regarding the teaching on the realization-path (praveśa-mārga), since this is the wondrous enlightenment, even the existence of a person within the teaching belongs to the provisional (upāya) category.
Thus, the reason for citing the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* is merely to attach it to that section, using two proofs to show that while those [two] realizations are real, the two teachings are [provisional].

Master Quan [Zhiyi] borrowed the meaning of "borrowing from others" to establish the *Shibu* (Section on Reality); this was merely based on the principle of classifying the teachings to their ultimate limits, taking the "realization of the fruit" as reality, and thus enabling him to cite it as proof.
However, if one grasps the present intent for classifying the teachings and the proofs, there is nowhere it will not reach.

Question: The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains only the three types [of teachings] and does not discuss them in terms of the "explanatory teaching" (*shuo*) and the "path of realization" (*zhengdao*); its meaning is therefore somewhat abbreviated. The *Qian* [the *Zhiguan Fuxing Zhuanhong Jueyao*] addresses this.

The *Wenbei* (Exhaustive Text) clarifies four types [of teachings], yet why does it refer back to them by saying they are "exhaustively" explained? In the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice), many responses to this objection have been offered: some say there is mutual variation in breadth and brevity; others say the names are brief while the text is extensive.

Neither of these accounts captures the underlying principle of the teaching and its verification (*śāsanādharma* and *adhigamadharma*). One should know that the *Fuxing* also clarifies the four types, as it says: [...text continues... The *Wenbei* clarifies the four types, yet why does it refer back to them by saying they are "exhaustively" explained? In the *Fuxing*, many responses to this objection have been offered: some say there is mutual variation in breadth and brevity; others say the names are brief while the text is extensive. Neither of these accounts captures the underlying principle of the teaching and its verification. One should know that the *Fuxing* also clarifies the four types, as it says:
The destruction of the twelve grades of ignorance is called "wondrous enlightenment" (*miao-jue*); this refers specifically to the path of realization (*zhengdao*).

Those of old did not understand that this particular stage resides within wondrous enlightenment; failing to recognize the four types of teaching and realization fully explained in the *Fuxing*, they vainly engaged in forced interpretations.
If one grasps this intent, the fourfold meaning is complete. Therefore, the citations from the texts are extensive, while the commentary on the *Jijie* is concise.

As for what you have raised as a doubt regarding the breadth [of the text], this objection is likewise unnecessary. From this, one can know that when Jingxi [Zhanran] took up his pen, he was straightforward and clear;

where has he ever been circuitous? It is simply that people do not understand and thus lose the Patriarch’s intent. Regarding the *Mohe zhiguan*, it says: "The *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) are both sudden and gradual.
Because those with a beginner's mind know the Middle Way, they are called 'sudden'; because they enter by traversing the skillful means, they are called 'gradual.'"

Is the name [of this teaching] that which is both gradual and sudden—the "sudden" of the Perfect-Complete Middle, or is it merely the Middle? If one says it is merely the Middle, it would not accord with the meaning of the "Sudden" in the present context.

If one claims it is the Perfect-Middle, how could a beginner know it? The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "The first three teachings do not know the principle of the Perfect. How is this point to be understood?
The answer is that traditionally it has been said that they know "merely the Middle," and that "Middle" [is the Perfect-Middle].
Because the essence of the Path-dharma is identical to that of the Perfect Middle, it is said to be "also sudden. Recently, some have claimed this is not so;

however, the statement here that "knowing the Middle is called 'also sudden'" specifically refers to the gradual and sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and clear observation) in order to distinguish between the partial and the perfect. One must take the Perfect Middle as the sudden.

Regarding the meaning of the "initial mind" of the Separate Teaching, there are two kinds: the initial mind of one who has received the teaching, and the initial [mind] of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

The mind is now discussed in relation to the first stage (*bhūmi*), which is also called the "initial mind. This is analogous to how the first dwelling is named the "dwelling of the initial arousal of the mind" (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*).
Here, it refers specifically to the first stage; because the realization of the Middle Way therein is identical to the Perfect [Teaching], it is termed "also sudden.

Thus, the subsequent text of the *Zhiguan* states: "Advancing to shatter ignorance and enter the first stage constitutes the realization of the sudden path. The *Fuxing* commentary notes: "The preceding three [stages] do not know the Perfect."

"Principle" (*li*) refers to the initial mind that receives the teaching. When both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) take the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) as "sudden," this refers precisely to the initial mind of the first stage.
However, while this interpretation may seem acceptable at first hearing, upon careful examination, it greatly misses the essential meaning;

there are many instances where it contradicts the texts and opposes the underlying principles. This is likely due to a failure to distinguish the specific doctrinal tenets of the distinct teachings (*biejiao*).

Regarding the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*), its doctrines and meanings are difficult to clarify. First, I shall elucidate the fundamental tenets of the Separate Teaching, and next, I shall point out the errors of others.

Now, as for the Separate Teaching: while both the Separate and Perfect Teachings equally expound the Middle Principle, discuss the Three Truths, refute ignorance (*avidyā*), manifest the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), and understand how the hundred realms manifest as Buddhas through the body of transformation, they also understand that within the one there are the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable there is the one.

First, regarding this teaching, those beginners who receive its instruction immediately understand that the Dharma-gates expounded concerning the merits of the fifty-two stages are not lacking in their perfect subtlety;

yet, just as in the *Avataṃsaka* assembly where all hear the Buddha’s preaching together and receive his intent, there remains a distinction between what is sequential and what is non-sequential, whereby two teachings are differentiated.
This is because the understanding of the distinct-capacity practitioners (bie-ren) has neither reached nor attained [the ultimate].

Regarding the fact that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) ultimately becomes distinct (biejiao), it is just as the various masters of antiquity have explained: the three bodies (trisambodhi) and the three virtues (triguṇa) are not themselves not perfect and subtle.
However, our school judges them all to belong to the Distinct Teaching because they do not discuss the inherent nature (xingju). Why is this so? Jingxi said:

"They only know the interpenetration at the level of the fruit, but do not know the fundamental principle of the nature of all sentient beings; though they know the perfect fusion of the one and the many..."

That which is called the inconceivable principle refers to the fact that these merits exist upon the future fruit; yet one does not realize that the initial mind and the stage of fruition are one, nor that the dharmas of the fruit are entirely present within the causal mind.
Although one anticipates the perfection of this principle at the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), this very anticipation causes the perfect fusion to become a succession of distinct stages.
Thus, while the name "immediacy" (*sahaja*) exists, the actual meaning of immediacy is absent; though one understands the Middle Way, it remains merely a conceptual judgment.
Its establishment is based solely on the provisional aspect of the teaching; because the Middle Way is manifested in the first stage, it is based solely on the ultimate reality.

Because the Middle Way understood therein is perfectly integrated and identical, it is "sudden" from the perspective of ultimate reality, as they are the same. Yet, because it is based solely on the provisional aspect of the teaching, it is also "gradual.
The fundamental tenets of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna) do not change; having examined and analyzed them repeatedly, I see that whenever students speak...
Regarding what is called "the Middle Alone" (*butong zhong*) in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*): it is like the moon beyond the clouds or a lotus emerging from the water.

Often, the Dharma-gates understood by those of the Separate Teaching are considered inferior to those of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). This is because those of the Shared Teaching understand that all phenomena are empty without needing exhaustive analysis;

they immediately know that all dharmas are illusory in their very substance and thus understand them as being identical with emptiness. How could this be compared to the Separate Teaching’s exposition of the Middle Way?

If one’s principle does not reach [this], then how can mere emptiness be lamented? One must understand that the Separate and Perfect [teachings] are such that two people may sit on the same seat, hear the Buddha preach the inconceivable principle together, and receive the Middle Way together—whereby both illumination and cessation are simultaneous, and the three virtues and three bodies are thoroughly understood without exception.
The reason they are divided into two teachings is because it is only when one directs the mind toward these wondrous qualities with the fruit as the goal that one is truly able [to realize them].

The realization of why this teaching possesses such perfect subtlety is that it is not because the dharmas of the mind reach what is otherwise unattainable that it becomes the practice cultivated by those of the Separate Teaching (Byōdō), which constitutes the practice of gradual stages (*anupūrvakrama*).
Many people are confused regarding the intent of this teaching. Next, to briefly point out the errors of others, there are four fallacies.
First, there is no principle that can be expressed if one claims that knowing the "Middle" at the initial mind refers to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
I do not yet understand what principle was expounded at the time this person received the teaching; for what period did he receive it?
That no fruit may be expected is truly lamentable. If one claims it was merely the "Middle" (but-mid), I do not yet know what constitutes that "mere Middle.

As discussed previously, such a person often fails to reach the level of the two masters of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), thereby contradicting the *Fuxingji* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) as explained therein.

This refers to the claim that while the understanding is sudden, the practice is gradual; it suggests that one merely knows the sudden principle, whereas practice must necessarily pass through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Now, if this "understanding" is said to be merely knowing the sudden principle, is this the understanding of the first bhūmi, or is it the understanding of a beginner who has just received the teachings?
If you say it is the first bhūmi, then since the first bhūmi has already realized the principle of perfect suddenness, why [is practice still required]?

Regarding the statement "only knowing it," one should verify that Jingxi [Zhiyuan] was specifically referring to those at the initial stage of receiving the teachings who are merely able to know this sudden principle but have not yet been able to practice according to that principle immediately; thus he said "only.

Is this not a definitive indication of the initial mind of receiving the teachings? It appears that this person has never read to the passage by Fuxing and has thus composed this erroneous interpretation.
A person with eyes who briefly understands how to read will surely know upon seeing this text that one must take the initial mind of receiving the teaching as the starting point;

how could it be that [the text] suddenly points to the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) as the "initial mind"? Could this possibly be the intended meaning of the *Zhi guan fu xing* (Auxiliary Practices of Calm and Insight)?
Therefore, we know that this interpretation is clearly erroneous. Third, there is confusion regarding "calm and insight" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), for calm and insight distinguish [the stages].
The provisional and the perfect encompass many preceding aspects. First, they are distinguished by means of the four propositions; next, they are distinguished by means of the four dharmas;
finally, they are distinguished by means of the indeterminate and so forth. As for the four propositions, they are distinguished by correlating principle with teaching.

Thus, in the *Fuxingzhuan* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings] are given the name "gradual" based on the intent of the teachings they establish, while the *Bie* (Distinct) Teaching is named "sudden" based on its understanding of the sudden principle—thus it is "sudden" in the fourth [category].
Within the Dharma, there are two kinds of fourfold dharmas (*catuṣka-dharma*). The first concerns the teaching, contemplation, practice, and realization. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:

"For now, we shall explain the four dharmas by means of the two paths of teaching and realization. It further states: "The preceding four dharmas distinguish the provisional from the real by contrasting them with the three dharmas [of contemplation, practice, and realization];

subsequently, they contrast the three dharmas of contemplation, practice, and entry into the teaching with the teaching itself to distinguish the provisional from the real. Thus, one knows that *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) is based upon these four.

Jujian states that if one receives the teaching at the initial stage of the path and immediately realizes this sudden principle upon attaining the first bhūmi, then the teaching is gradual while the principle is sudden;

thus it is called both "sudden" and "gradual. This distinction between the gradual and the sudden applies specifically to the stages of teaching and realization, reaching its full application at the time of the first bhūmi when one realizes the actual principle;

this is what is termed the "sudden" stage. Prior to the bhūmis, it is also gradual. As for the four subsequent dharmas, they are distinguished by the presence of the teaching but the absence of the person.

Each category of the sudden and gradual teachings has its own specific meaning for distinguishing between the sudden and the gradual; one cannot take a single category from among the four propositions and apply it universally below to claim that the first stage constitutes the "beginner's mind.
Is this not a violation of the text of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Mohe zhiguan*)? Regarding the fourth error concerning the phrase "the beginner's mind" in the context of stages and positions:
one must point to the initial reception of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as being the "beginner's mind," as is stated in the subsequent section of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.

The text states that within the general and specific [teachings], from the initial mind up to the final mind, when speaking of the final mind in contrast to the initial mind, the "initial mind" must refer to the very first moment of the beginning.
That our school has never taken the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) as the "initial mind," yet openly contradicts this by fabricating such an interpretation—how laughable!
One must understand that even in this teaching, the stage of the Sudden (*tun*) is established at the First Ground; thus, the initial mind is indeed capable [of attaining realization].

The "knower" refers to the mind that first receives the teaching; one immediately knows that above the initial stage (prathamā-bhūmi), there exists this aspiration for sudden realization, which aims at the realization of the dharma of perfect interfusion. Therefore, this is pointed out as the "subsequent fruit.

The term "subsequent fruit" extends all the way to wondrous enlightenment (miao-jue), for all are what is aspired to and pointed toward by the initial mind. Thus, we know that this interpretation is truly without error.
The error of misapprehending what has been received and misleading others is a fault of no small magnitude. Regarding the doctrines of Teaching and Realization, many hold divergent opinions;

this is entirely due to a failure to comprehend the specific intent of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). What is clarified here accords with the meaning of our Patriarch’s intention; future worthies and sages will surely possess the discernment to appreciate it.

Regarding the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, some have asked: "The text discusses the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), yet the title designates 'expedient means' (*upāya*). Why are the general and the specific not consistent?
In the past, commentators have offered divergent theories, proliferating various systems of interpretation, each filling its chapters with elegant prose. I [shall now address this].
Whenever I have investigated and deliberated upon these various explanations, I found them to be circuitous rather than direct and inconsistent with the unified intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Upon examining them closely, I saw that the sutra texts do not explicitly designate [the teaching] as "ultimate reality" (bhūtatathatā), but instead specifically title it "expedient means" (upāya); there must be a profound reason for this.
For if it were designated as ultimate reality, one would find that the general and specific categories within the sutras would lack coherence. Why is this so? Śākyamuni...
Venerable one, it was from the presence of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū that you established this connection with this class of beings;
through various means of ripening them over the course of immeasurable kalpas, employing countless compassionate and skillful expedients to gather and guide them,
you have protected them until this day, so that their minds have now become fully matured, and upon hearing what the Buddha has taught, they do not give rise to slander.
The fundamental aspiration for which the Tathāgata appeared in the world has today reached fulfillment; his exerted efforts have not been in vain.

How could he not be joyful and filled with delight? Therefore, as we approach the bestowal of the prophecy, he first extols the merit of his skillful means and recounts the power of his guidance and gathering from the past. For this reason, this sutra is truly the pinnacle of all calculations.
Therefore, I say that since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have used various causes and conditions, parables, and verbal teachings, as well as countless skillful means, to guide sentient beings.

In each of the chapters on the five Buddhas, it is stated that by means of countless skillful means and through the power of such expedients, I have differentiated the single Buddha Vehicle into three for the sake of discourse, so as to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom. This is my own expedient; all other Buddhas do likewise.

For this reason, when the Tathāgata earnestly extols that which is praised, he does not praise the ultimate reality, but rather praises the merit of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), which is difficult to accomplish.
At the beginning of the chapter, the text praises these skillful means, stating: "The gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
This refers to the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of what is taught according to suitability; this too is [the result of] skillful means.
At the end of this chapter, he offers praise, saying: "The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus; by means of ten billion skillful means (*upāya*), they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Thus, one knows that from beginning to end, this entire chapter is a praise of skillful means.

Although the scriptural text of the "Chapter on Skillful Means" explains what is manifested as the ultimate reality (*tattva*), the merit of this revelation is entirely due to the power of skillful means.

That we have reached this point was because, in the past, when the provisional teaching was being established, [the Buddha] concealed and guarded [the truth], not allowing us to perceive it, so that we remained in the City of Transformation, believing it to be real.
Only today, upon hearing this teaching, do we realize that the Tathāgata’s skillful application of expedient means has brought about our awakening;
we now understand that what we previously realized was not the ultimate truth. This was our own fault, not the World-Honored One’s. Had it not been for this...
By what means did you skillfully employ such transformations today to obtain such great benefit?

Only now do I realize that the Tathāgata is truly a Great Teacher who guides and leads all beings to enter the Buddha-wisdom. This is precisely what the Buddha praises; it is praise for the merit of his skillful means (*upāya*).

That the conditions have been stirred to resonance is likewise a debt owed to the transformation of skillful means. It is through skillful means that one attains accord with the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The merit of skillful means (*upāya*) is truly difficult to conceive; therefore, it is that which is earnestly praised.

Is it not fitting that the compiler of this sutra, having perfectly grasped the Buddha’s mind, designates this chapter as "Skillful Means"? How could one say that the discourse on reality lacks coherence between its general and specific aspects?
To further clarify this, let us borrow a worldly analogy: it is like a skilled general who has been entrusted with the heavy responsibilities of the state.

To lead a million-strong army against enemies and eliminate a host of a million fierce raiders—where the lives and deaths of millions and the survival or ruin of the state and its altars of soil and grain all rest in the hands of a single commander—if one’s strategic planning is not profound, one’s wisdom and tactics not extensive, and one’s maneuvers not kept secret when applied according to the moment, how can such a person bear this heavy responsibility? Or perhaps... [text ends]
When one is not harmed by what is unfavorable, is that not a matter of no small importance?

Furthermore, to defeat the invaders, destroy the enemy, establish great meritorious achievements, accomplish the state’s great affairs, preserve the army, and stabilize the altars of state—how could the commander-in-chief not feel joy and delight?
Once the merit is established, he can stand before the vast assembly and praise his strategic ingenuity; such skillful means are indeed capable of achieving success.
When a great matter approaches, it is precisely the time for strategic planning; what is used in secrecy must by no means be leaked.
Once a clever stratagem has been perfected, only then may one proclaim and praise it before the multitude.

Examples such as Sun Bin’s reduction of the cooking fires, Han Xin’s abandonment of the banners, Zhang Lu’s concealment of his name, and Chen Ping’s counter-questioning—all these were the skillful secrets of superior generals capable of serving the state.

The pacification of the realm and the stabilization of one’s vocation apply to the Buddha as well; yet, because the Buddha’s transformations are inconceivable, one must not judge his sacred functions by worldly trifles.
For those who have not yet fully realized them, he borrows mundane events as analogies to serve as skillful means for sentient beings, employing expedient devices to shatter the armies of Māra.
He acts precisely according to the timing and circumstances, keeping his methods secret and hidden so that they are not perceived; now that his work has been accomplished, [he reveals it].

Coming to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the "Appreciation of Merit" (*Puṇyaparyāya*) and the "Entrustment" (*Parīndanā*) chapters are both called "expedient means" (*upāya*), which is precisely to manifest the "reality" (*bhūta*).
Since expedient means possesses the function of manifesting reality, it is for this reason that they are so earnestly praised. How could one not find these chapter titles truly magnificent?
How can one raise objections on the grounds that the general and the specific are not consistent? If the scribe were to instead title these chapters as "Reality," [the meaning would be lost].

Regarding the formation of the general and specific [categories], they do not extend to the present. Now, our own school (Shanjia) explains "expedient means" (*upāya*) through three types, which most closely accords with the Buddha’s intent.
Although there are these three types, all take the Three Teachings as the expedient means; the Three Teachings are one, though they differ between the past and the present.

In the past, these were employed as skillful devices to guide and transform beings according to their capacities; this application is called "dharma-function. If it were not for this function, by what means could [beings] be reached?
Today, having attained entry into the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), these three teachings are pointed out as the gates for entering reality; they are called "capable of leading.

Although they were employed in the past, sentient beings were entirely unaware of them. Only now, through this explicit teaching, do we finally understand that these skillful means (*upāya*)—though the three teachings are designated as such—are in their very essence the ultimate truth.
Therefore, these skillful means receive the title of "Secret and Sublime" (*guhyamandala*). In former times, they were not so named.
Taking the one as three, today we know that the three are entirely the one; because they are categorized from the perspective of the three, it is called the "secret and wondrous skillful means.

This is precisely the three within the one. It is like a skilled general who employs such ingenuity: at the moment of actual application, he devises strategies according to what is appropriate, which is called "dharma-function" (*dharmaprayoga*).
If it were not for this stratagem, by what means could success be achieved? This is called "being able to penetrate. Since...
Having already achieved success, he praised before the assembly what he had previously employed;

since that which was used has now succeeded, he now provides a classification and thus explains the title by means of the secret and wondrous. This very title is precisely what is praised today as the "expedient means" (*upāya*).
What is praised here is not a separate expedient means, but is rather the skillful art (*kauśalya*) employed previously. Thus, these three explanations all employ the three teachings.
The first two [meanings] serve as skillful means (*upāya*) to interpret previous sutras, while the latter one correctly accords with the present chapter.

Since these skillful means possess the function of revealing the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), this chapter is specifically titled "Skillful Means. This interpretation by Tiantai perfectly accords with the Buddha’s intention and deeply conforms to the meaning of the sutra;
how could it be compared to the so-called "constant amidst the impermanent" or "internal stillness amidst external change" of the ancient masters?

Is this not the same as what was said on that previous day? Furthermore, do you realize that the discourse currently being presented can it truly be placed on equal footing with the shallow and crude arguments of those former scholars?
Nevertheless, even in the past, the commentaries were seen to state at every section that the provisional (upāya) possesses the merit of manifesting the ultimate reality;
therefore, the title and chapter headings were derived from the provisional, yet it was asserted that the provisional is itself the truth.

In truth, although the name is designated based on absolute transcendence (*atyanta-apekṣā*), the intention behind the designation of these expedient means (*upāya*) is entirely to indicate the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).

This is because expedient means are themselves reality; it is intended that those with the appropriate capacity (*tad-yogyatā*) should perceive these expedients and understand them as being truly real.

Thus, commentators who skillfully expound the teachings provide such an interpretation, which is why there is the doctrine that both name and essence do not shift. If one considers what has been stated above...
Miaoyi’s analysis of these points merely captures the principle of the three being of one essence;

it has not yet discerned the reason for the Tathāgata’s earnest praise nor the intention behind the chapter title as designated by the compiler of the sutra. I request those with clear vision to examine this in detail.
As for discussing the revelation based on the three types [of teachings] and explaining the title according to various texts, this was the work of former scholars.

My own work is already detailed and complete; now I am concerned only that what has been taught since ancient times may not accord with the purport of the sutras, the Buddha’s intention, and the Patriarchs’ intention.
Fearing that [the truth] might be submerged and lost, I have briefly raised these points to rescue them from being drowned.
I hope that those on the same path will together open the gate of skillful means and penetrate deeply into the treasury of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who receive the Dharma of our Buddha and establish the practice of cultivation must, by means of the three contemplations, treat the three kinds of delusions, realize the principle of the three truths, and manifest the bodies of the three virtues;
this is the ultimate essential. The single school of Tiantai establishes four types of teachings to categorize and encompass [the Buddha’s doctrines].
Throughout my life, I have practiced with reason and wisdom, yet there is nothing I have not thoroughly investigated; I have long harbored a private doubt regarding this:

if the teachings are that which express (*nengquan*) and principle is that which is expressed (*suquan*), then since principle must necessarily exist, how can it be that the *San-zang* and *Tong* (Shared) teachings both express the "True Principle" (*zhentili*), while the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings both express the "Middle Principle" (*zhongli*), yet as for the "Conventional Principle" (*sulili*), there appears to be no teaching that expresses it? Furthermore, I have privately doubted that since delusions are threefold, [the teachings must correspond].

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*), those within the internal realm take view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi*) and afflictive ignorance (*kleśa-avidyā*) as their causes, while those outside the internal realm take fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) as their cause.
As for the "dust-like sands" (*rajas-tulya-saṃyojana*), to which realm do they belong? Thus, the dust-like sands pervade both the internal and external realms.

Furthermore, since those two types of delusion have limitations regarding the internal and external, why do the dust-like sands pervade both the internal and the external? Moreover, I have heard that former sages have [categorized] the dust-like sands...
Disputes over whether [the seeds] lead to rebirth or do not lead to rebirth were so numerous and conflicting that they could not reach a single conclusion.

Thereupon, I examined the ancestral texts and researched ancient expositions, until I saw that the ancestral writings were extremely clear; it was only that people of the past were themselves ignorant. Only the *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the Profound School) contains the words:

"The layers of *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned through cultivation) are as numerous as dust motes or grains of sand. These two sentences alone provide a profound understanding of the essence of delusion. Regarding this, I...

The meaning cannot remain silent; I shall attempt to briefly elucidate it. First, I will present the former explanations, followed by the orthodox position. Regarding the former, there were two views:

one holds that [the afflictions] "lead to birth" (*prakarṣa-janman*), and the other holds that they do not. As for those who maintain they lead to birth: they say that the delusions of *dṛṣṭi* and *saṃyojana* (view-delusions and thought-delusions) lead to birth in the *sahā-loka-dhātu* (the realm of shared existence);

the delusions of *rajas* and *sūtra* (dust-like and sand-like delusions) lead to birth in the *upāya-bhūmi* (the stage of skillful means); and the delusions of *avidyā* (ignorance) lead to birth in the *tathatā-nisyanda-phala-bhūmi* (the stage of the fruition flowing from suchness). According to the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Text): "If..."

If the four abidings do not exist, the birth of the *parīcchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) does not arise; if ignorance does not exist, skillful means (*upāya*) do not arise; if nescience (*avidyā*) does not exist, the true retribution does not arise.

If that which draws forth birth does not exist, how can there be the obstruction of the *rajas-aṇu* (dust-sand-like hindrances)? How can the transformation and guidance be blocked by *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* afflictions?

When the delusions of *darśana* and *bhāvanā* persist, they draw forth birth within the three realms. Once the delusions of *darśana* and *bhāvanā* are shattered, the delusion of nescience manifests, moistening the birth of skillful means.

When the delusion of ignorance is first shattered in its first grade, one immediately gives rise to the true retribution [land]; this is verified by knowing that the "dust-sands" [afflictions] have no meaning of "producing" [birth].
The previously cited text is a teaching concerning the three delusions in relation to the lands;

because there is the meaning of "producing" or "non-producing" as in the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, these three delusions constitute "producing," whereas the absence of these three delusions constitutes the three "non-productions. Thus, the "dust-sands" are contrasted with the land of skillful means (*upāya*).
It is not that the "dust-sands" (grains of sand) do not pull forth the arising of existence; for those who raise objections might ask:

"If it is said that the dust-sands do not pull forth arising, why does the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* state that 'immeasurable grasping at signs brings about immeasurable birth-and-death, and immeasurable dust-sands invite immeasurable retributions, such that immeasurable ignorance receives immeasurable retribution-bodies'? Since it is already stated that they 'invite immeasurable retributions' [the dust-sands must indeed have such power]."
Is it not the case that there are commentators who explain [the phrase] "drawing forth" (*ākarṣaṇa*) as "producing existence" (*bhava*)? They say:

"What is called 'invoking retribution' does not mean drawing forth or actually creating retribution; rather, it is because Bodhisattvas emerge from the provisional state to transform sentient beings, shatter the *cusha* delusions, enter the realm of birth and death, and employ the means of 'identical activity' (*samānārthatā*) to provisionally undergo retribution. This is indeed what was written by a renowned master of recent times.

Thus he explained it; his disciples have transmitted this as a profound treatise. I have often lamented that they are so obscure, and only upon being shown the True Doctrine (Zhengzong) do their errors become apparent.

Furthermore, one must understand that the "dust-sands" [of afflictions] have no separate essence from delusion; they are entirely designated as "dust-sands" based on the medicinal methods for the diseases of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions).

How is this known? It is because of what is shown in the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation): [The text continues with the citation from the *Mohe zhiguan*. I have translated the provided passage above. If you provide the remainder of the text, I shall continue the translation accordingly.
There are three aspects to emerging from the provisional [teachings]: namely, knowing the illness, identifying the medicine, and the method of administering the medicine.

"Knowing the illness" means knowing the illnesses of affliction and views (*kleśa* and *dṛṣṭi*) of all sentient beings; knowing the root of affliction and views; and knowing the causes and conditions, duration, proximity, and frequency of affliction and views.
"Identifying the medicine" means there is mundane medicine, supramundane medicine, and the supreme-supramundane medicine. This refers to the method of administering the medicine.

As for the method, one must be able to observe the capacities of others and provide medicine according to their ailments. First, one must personally understand both the medicines and the ailments, and furthermore, master the methods of administering the medicine.
One should provide it according to the specific ailment to cause the other to take joy in it, so that they may be cured by taking it accordingly.
If one can thoroughly comprehend these three—namely, the ailment and so forth—it is called "shattering the dust-like [delusions]. If these three are not understood, they are termed "afflictions."
Because the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*) are both general and specific, the *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like) delusions are likewise categorized as internal and external.
If one can distinguish those that are general to both views and thought, and administer medicine to treat them, one breaks the *rajas-reṇu* within the realm;

if one can distinguish those that are specific to views and thought, and administer medicine to treat them, one then breaks the *rajas-reṇu* outside the realm. Therefore, it is known that the *rajas-reṇu* has no separate essential substance (*svabhāva*); it refers to [the aforementioned afflictions].
Being skillfully able to distinguish between the characteristics of the medicines and diseases of view and thought is termed "the Bodhisattva who shatters the sands of dust.

Since benefiting sentient beings is his primary concern, he studies the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to extensively distinguish medicines and diseases for the sake of all beings.

Although he has not yet shattered the ignorance beyond the realms (*dhātu*), he is already able to study the fourfold Four Noble Truths and the sixteen aspects of the provisional teachings, reaching up to the [First] Ground.

Only when one dwells [in this state] and shatters even a single grade of ignorance can it be called true benefit. If this is so, then the dust-like and river-sand-like delusions belong to the realm of others;

they are the afflictions of view-delusion and thought-delusion (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-āsrava*), the causes and conditions of view and thought, the duration of view and thought, the frequency of view and thought, as well as the medicine for treating view and thought.
As for why these cannot pull one into rebirth, it is because my own view and thought have already preceded them.
Having already severed [the afflictions] themselves, one has not yet been able to discern how the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *kleśa*) of others pull forth one’s own birth.

Therefore, one knows that among the delusions belonging to one’s own portion, only the two types—view-delusion and ignorance (*avidyā*)—are capable of pulling forth birth within and beyond the realms.
To desire the extinction of these delusions, one cultivates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*); by severing these two delusions, one’s own practice reaches fulfillment.

It is said that while one practices oneself solely within the realm of emptiness, the office of a Bodhisattva lies in benefiting others. From the very first arousal of the mind, bodhi is the foundation;
with the vow to deliver infinite sentient beings, one acts in accordance with this original intent.

Therefore, it is necessary to analyze for others the various layers of afflictions—both those of views and those of thought—so that all people may grow weary of and depart from birth and death, forever emerging from the cycle of saṃsāra. If...

Furthermore, one cannot thoroughly penetrate these gates of views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) while remaining mired in the sands of phenomena; how then could one serve as a guide for sentient beings?

Thus it is said that "the sands of phenomena constitute an obstruction. For the sake of others, one makes distinctions to treat their illnesses and break through their birth-and-death.

Because others do not know that these are illnesses, they invite immeasurable birth-and-death and undergo immeasurable retributions; therefore, [the teaching is directed at] all sentient beings as numerous as dust-sands.
It is called the "view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) within the stage of the Bodhisattva who has severed delusions; it is termed the "afflictions as numerous as motes of dust.

If people do not see this, they immediately claim that the Bodhisattva invites his own retribution through these dust-like afflictions and drags himself into his own cycle of birth and death—how great is their error!

If one understands this meaning, the text on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness will be brilliantly clarified and all doubts resolved. How could one then enter the realm of birth and death while merely engaging in "commonality of purpose" (*samānārthatā*)?

To summarize and resolve those textual passages: Alas, why did this master propagate such views? Regarding the previous two assertions—that "dust-like afflictions" (*rajas*) lead to rebirth—these are entirely mistaken in their intent.
They not only misinterpret the scriptural passages concerning non-arising (*anutpāda*), but they also fail to recognize the essential nature of the dust-like afflictions.
As explained previously, even if one knows that the dust-like afflictions do not lead to rebirth, [the former view remains erroneous].

Regarding the statement that "the sands of dust have no meaning of moistening," and the principle of "not knowing what it is to lack [moistening]," both stem from not understanding that this delusion has no separate self-substance.

If the essence of delusion were real, this principle would be self-evident; therefore, one knows that the principle expounded by our school’s teachings refers only to True Suchness (bhūtatathatā) and the Middle Way, and does not refer to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Furthermore, the realm of birth moistened by delusion consists only of the internal and external; this principle is manifest.

Whether practicing for oneself or transforming others, regarding the teachings of principle and wisdom, the severance of delusions, the three contemplations, and the three truths—there is nothing that is not clearly revealed.

As for the various afflictions and their residual habits (*vāsanā*), their essence and characteristics may occasionally be encountered; however, I have long lamented that the characteristics of these *rajas* (dust-like) afflictions have rarely been clarified.
